title: Bolted down or free on ice: which block reaches the floor first? Free wedge 0.39 s, bolted 0.49 s
description:
Bolted down or free on ice: which block reaches the floor first? One scene, side view, two panels on one clock. In each a 1 kg block (a 6 cm cube, treated as a point mass at its centre) rests at the top of a 30 degree wedge of 1 kg, 30 cm up, 60 cm of slope, no friction between the block and the wedge. On top the wedge is bolted to the floor. Below the same wedge sits free on ice, no friction under it either, and both blocks are let go at the same instant. A floor pad stops each block at the foot of the slope with no bounce, and a buffer on the ice stops the free wedge at its landing position. Both runs are integrated by classical RK4 at 10000 steps per second (dt = 1e-04 s) with the normal force solved from the contact constraint at every stage, the floor crossing located by bisection inside the step, checked against the closed forms and a half-step rerun. Shown at 1/8 speed on a 10 s cycle, 4 drops in 40 s. Deterministic, no seed.

Measured:
- bolted wedge: the block accelerates along the slope at g sin a = 4.9035 m/s^2 and reaches the floor at sqrt(2 L / a) = 0.494695 s = 0.49 s, moving at 2.4257 m/s; it presses the wedge with N = m g cos a = 8.4931 N, 0.8660 of its weight; RK4 against the closed form diff +2.1e-15 s, 4947 steps
- free wedge on ice: the block accelerates along the slope at (M + m) g sin a / (M + m sin^2 a) = 7.8456 m/s^2, exactly 1.6000 times the bolted value, and reaches the floor at 0.391091 s = 0.39 s, 1.2649 times sooner (exactly sqrt(1.6)), 103.6 ms earlier; RK4 against the closed form diff +4.4e-16 s, 3911 steps
- the free wedge accelerates back at A = m g sin a cos a / (M + m sin^2 a) = 3.3972 m/s^2 and slides back 25.9808 cm = 26 cm at 1.3286 m/s; the block moves 25.9808 cm forward and 30.00 cm down in the lab (equal masses split the 51.96 cm run), on a path 49.1066 degrees below horizontal instead of 30; at the floor it moves at 2.0295 m/s (vx 1.3286, vy 1.5342 down)
- the free block presses the wedge with N = m M g cos a / (M + m sin^2 a) = 6.7945 N, 0.6928 of its weight, against 0.8660 on the bolted wedge
- when the free block lands at 0.3911 s the bolted block is at 0.3750 m of 0.600 m along its slope, 62.5 percent of the way
- horizontal momentum of block plus free wedge within 0.0e+00 kg m/s; energy: m g h = 2.9421 J against 2.9421 J of kinetic energy at the floor in both runs (diffs +1.4e-13 and +2.4e-13 J); contact residual within 7.5e-15 and 1.4e-14 m; half-step rerun (dt = 5e-05 s) moves the floor times by +9.7e-15 and -5.2e-15 s
- the drop (real time after the release), free against bolted: 0.1000 s: 3.92 against 2.45 cm along the slope; 0.2000 s: 15.69 against 9.81 cm; 0.3000 s: 35.31 against 22.07 cm; 0.3911 s: the free block on the floor, the bolted block at 37.5 cm; 0.4947 s: the bolted block on the floor
- a heavier wedge, same 1 kg block, 30 degrees: 2 kg, a ratio 1.3333, floor at 0.4284 s, wedge back 17.32 cm, pressing 0.7698 of its weight; 5 kg: 1.1429, 0.4627 s, 8.66 cm, 0.8248; 10 kg: 1.0732, 0.4775 s, 4.72 cm, 0.8449; a lighter wedge of 0.5 kg: 2.0000, 0.3498 s, 34.64 cm, 0.5774
- other angles, the same 30 cm drop, equal masses: 20 degrees, a ratio 1.7905, free 0.5405 s against bolted 0.7232 s, wedge back 41.21 cm; 45 degrees, 1.3333, 0.3029 against 0.3498 s, 15.00 cm; 60 degrees, 1.1429, 0.2672 against 0.2856 s, 8.66 cm

Why: on the bolted wedge the block only gets the part of gravity along the slope, g sin a. On the free wedge the block pushes the wedge out from under it, so the block falls on a steeper path (49 degrees instead of 30) and the contact needs less force to hold it on the slope (0.69 of its weight instead of 0.87). The acceleration along the slope becomes (M + m) g sin a / (M + m sin^2 a); with equal masses that is 2 / (1 + sin^2 a) = 1.6 times g sin a. The fall time scales as one over the square root of the acceleration, so the free block lands sqrt(1.6) = 1.26 times sooner: 0.39 s against 0.49 s for 60 cm of slope. A heavier wedge moves less and the gain shrinks; a lighter wedge moves more and the gain grows.

Rerun sims/wedge/wedge.py with projects/wedge/manifest.json and you get these numbers exactly.

Made end to end by an AI agent: simulation, footage, voice, music, and edit.
